xxHash: Yann Collet's [xxHash](https://cyan4973.github.io/xxHash/) family — among the fastest non-cryptographic hashes available, with excellent distribution. [`xxh3_64`](#xxh3_64) is a sensible modern default; the 128-bit variants ([`xxh3_128`](#xxh3_128), [`xxh3_128_hex`](#xxh3_128_hex)) give you more headroom against accidental collisions and a portable hex digest format used by [Python xxhash](https://pypi.org/project/xxhash/) and [xxhash-rust](https://docs.rs/xxhash-rust/latest/xxhash_rust/).
RapidHash: [RapidHash](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash) is purpose-built for raw 64-bit throughput while keeping competitive distribution quality. Frequently the fastest published 64-bit non-cryptographic hash on x86_64 — reach for [`rapidhash`](#rapidhash) when [`xxh3_64`](#xxh3_64)'s speed isn't quite enough. [`rapidhash_micro`](#rapidhash_micro) and [`rapidhash_nano`](#rapidhash_nano) are the upstream compact variants, for matching systems that use them.
MurmurHash3: Austin Appleby's [MurmurHash3](https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher) — a battle-tested non-cryptographic hash used across many distributed systems. Choose [`murmurhash3_32`](#murmurhash3_32), [`murmurhash3_128`](#murmurhash3_128), or [`murmurhash3_x64_128`](#murmurhash3_x64_128) when you need to interoperate with an existing standard MurmurHash3 consumer. To match Spark's `hash()`, which is *not* standard MurmurHash3, use [`spark_hash`](#spark_hash).
wyhash & komihash: Two compact, very fast 64-bit hashes popular in hash-table and language-runtime implementations: [wyhash](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash) ([`wyhash`](#wyhash), final version 4) and [komihash](https://github.com/avaneev/komihash) ([`komihash`](#komihash), version 5). Use them to match a system that already stores these hashes.
SipHash: [SipHash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SipHash) is a *keyed* hash: with a secret 128-bit key, an attacker who doesn't know the key can't craft colliding inputs, which protects hash tables and partitioners from hash-flooding. [`siphash24`](#siphash24) is the standard SipHash-2-4; [`siphash13`](#siphash13) is the faster SipHash-1-3 used by Rust's standard library and CPython. Neither is a substitute for a cryptographic digest or MAC — use [crypto](/products/extensions/crypto) for those.
CRC-32C & FNV-1a: Classic checksum and hash formats that other systems embed: [CRC-32C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_redundancy_check) (Castagnoli), used by iSCSI, ext4, Google Cloud Storage object checksums and many storage formats, and [FNV-1a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler%E2%80%93Noll%E2%80%93Vo_hash_function), a tiny byte-at-a-time hash common in older code.
Matching other systems: Functions that reproduce another system's hash exactly — same algorithm, same byte encoding, same seed and same signed or unsigned result — so DuckDB can compute keys, buckets and partitions that line up with [BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery), [Apache Spark](https://spark.apache.org/), [Apache Kafka](https://kafka.apache.org/), [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/) and [ClickHouse](https://clickhouse.com/). Each is tested against values produced by the real system.
Consistent hashing: Assign keys to a number of buckets so that changing the bucket count moves as few keys as possible. [`jump_hash`](#jump_hash) moves only about 1/(n + 1) of the keys when growing from n to n + 1 buckets, where `hash % n` would move almost all of them.
